articles.title: Safety and Tolerability of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors: A State-of-the-Art Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is) have evolved from glucose-lowering agents to foundational therapies for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease, with substantial benefits for cardiovascular, kidney, and survival outcomes. As their indications continue to expand, a comprehensive understanding of their safety and tolerability has become increasingly important for optimizing patient care. Building on our recent state-of-the-art review of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, this review provides a contemporary synthesis of the evidence on the safety and tolerability of SGLT-2is. We critically appraise data from randomized controlled trials, cardiovascular and kidney outcome trials, pharmacovigilance databases, large observational studies, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The available evidence demonstrates that SGLT-2is have a favorable overall safety profile, with genital mycotic infections representing the most consistently observed adverse event. Volume depletion and euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis remain clinically important but are uncommon and are largely preventable through appropriate patient selection, patient education, and temporary treatment interruption during high-risk clinical situations. Fournier's gangrene should be regarded as a very rare but serious complication requiring prompt recognition and treatment. In contrast, randomized trials and meta-analyses generally indicate a reduced risk of acute kidney injury, while evidence concerning fracture, lower-limb amputation, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and cancer is less definitive. Although consistent class-wide increases in these latter outcomes have not been established, uncommon or agent-specific risks cannot be excluded, particularly where event numbers are small or follow-up is limited. Overall, treatment discontinuation because of adverse events is low across major cardiovascular, heart failure, and kidney outcome trials, supporting the excellent tolerability of this therapeutic class. Comparative evidence suggests only modest differences among individual SGLT-2is, although definitive conclusions remain limited by the absence of direct, large, randomized head-to-head trials. We also summarize practical strategies for adverse-event mitigation, monitoring, temporary treatment interruption, and individualized patient selection. As the clinical applications of SGLT-2is continue to broaden, ongoing pharmacovigilance, inclusive clinical trials, and comparative safety studies will be essential to further refine their benefit-risk profile and optimize their safe use across diverse patient populations.

articles.title: Translational resilience in intravaginal HIV prevention and multipurpose prevention technologies: formulation, exposure, and implementation barriers.
articles.abstract: Intravaginal HIV prevention has progressed from early nonspecific microbicides to antiretroviral gels, films, inserts, and intravaginal rings, alongside emerging biologic agents and multipurpose prevention technologies (MPTs). Despite substantial advances in antiviral potency and formulation technology, translation from pharmaceutical development to consistent clinical protection has remained uneven, indicating that API activity or dosage-form performance alone is insufficient to explain clinical outcomes. This review critically examines the development of intravaginal HIV prevention and MPT products through a mechanistic pharmaceutical perspective, focusing on the relationships between controllable product attributes, drug release and transport, the cervicovaginal environment, compartment-specific pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD), and product use. Historical microbicide and antiretroviral programs are examined as translational case studies to identify how mucosal safety, local exposure and use-dependent drug delivery contributed to divergent clinical outcomes. The review further evaluates how cervicovaginal fluid, semen, mucus, epithelial barriers, hormonal state, microbiome composition, and inflammation can modify formulation behavior and drug transport; how API physicochemistry, solid state, drug loading, drug-polymer partitioning, and diffusivity constrain formulation architecture and release; and how these relationships differ among gels, films, inserts, sustained-release devices, MPTs, and biologic delivery systems. Particular attention is given to the distinction between drug incorporation, release, tissue transport, and pharmacologically relevant exposure, and to the additional challenges created when multiple APIs require different release rates, biological compartments, or durations of action. Platform characteristics are further considered in relation to the exposure patterns and product-use conditions they are intended to support. By integrating formulation science with cervicovaginal physiology, PK/PD, and clinical experience, this review provides a mechanistic basis for identifying where intravaginal prevention systems lose translational performance and which formulation-transport-exposure relationships require stronger evidence to support more reproducible clinical protection.

articles.title: Topical drug delivery for androgenetic alopecia: from hair follicle targeting to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is the most prevalent form of hair loss worldwide, yet current therapies remain limited by suboptimal efficacy, poor patient adherence, systemic adverse effects, and inadequate drug accumulation within diseased hair follicles. Increasing evidence indicates that AGA is a multifactorial disorder involving androgen signaling, oxidative stress, inflammation, stem cell dysfunction, vascular impairment, and follicular microenvironment remodeling, highlighting the need for localized, multi-mechanistic therapeutic strategies. In this context, topical delivery systems are being developed to increase drug exposure within disease-relevant follicular and perifollicular compartments and prolong local residence, while seeking to limit systemic exposure. This review summarizes the pathophysiological basis of AGA, current pharmacological therapies, and recent advances in topical delivery using nanocarriers, microneedles, ionic liquids, deep eutectic solvents, and stimuli-responsive systems. We further highlight rational design principles for hair follicle-targeted delivery, focusing on particle size optimization, surface engineering, biomimetic carriers, and microenvironment-responsive release. Finally, we discuss the evolving clinical pipeline, commercialization of emerging technologies, and the major translational challenges that need be addressed for successful clinical implementation. This review provides a comprehensive framework for the rational design of next-generation precision topical therapies for AGA and offers perspectives for accelerating their clinical translation.

articles.title: Pharmacological targeting of ANO1/TMEM16A in cancer: from channel inhibition to protein downregulation.
articles.abstract: Anoctamin 1 (ANO1/TMEM16A) is a calcium-activated chloride channel increasingly recognized as a compelling pharmacological target in oncology. Beyond its role in chloride flux, ANO1 has also been proposed to exert signaling-associated or scaffold-like functions in selected malignancies, including head and neck, breast, and lung cancers. Although pharmacological studies have progressed from broad inhibitors to selective probes and natural products, a critical need has emerged for a rigorous standard to evaluate these agents. A central challenge is distinguishing acute conductance blockade from protein-level downregulation, as these mechanisms may produce distinct biological outcomes. Channel inhibition suppresses ion flux while potentially leaving ANO1-associated protein complexes intact, whereas protein reduction may affect both conductance-dependent and signaling-associated functions; however, the extent to which these functions are mechanistically independent remains incompletely established. Consequently, regulation of ANO1 stability is emerging as a promising therapeutic strategy in tumors with high ANO1 expression and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activation. However, in clinically relevant EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer models, the role of ANO1 should be interpreted cautiously. Current evidence supports ANO1 as a context-dependent preclinical vulnerability rather than an established mechanism for overcoming osimertinib resistance. To address methodological inconsistencies in the field, this review summarizes ANO1 cancer pharmacology and proposes a conservative operational evidence framework. By establishing strict validation criteria, we classify ANO1 modulators into functional inhibitors, dual modulators, protein-level downregulators, and protein-stability modulators while defining evidence requirements for bona fide targeted degrader designation.

articles.title: Receptor-Guided Nanomedicine for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Linking Target Biology, Nanocarrier Design, and Translation.
articles.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovitis and progressive joint destruction. Although current therapies improve disease control, inadequate lesion selectivity, heterogeneous responses, and systemic toxicity remain important limitations. Receptor-guided nanomedicine offers a strategy to align drug delivery with disease-relevant cell populations and pathological processes. This Review examines how receptor biology and pharmacological characteristics shape ligand selection, carrier architecture, payload choice, administration route, and microenvironment-responsive design in RA nanotherapy. Particular emphasis is placed on folate receptor-β (FRβ) and CD44, which represent the most extensively investigated receptor axes for activated macrophages and broader synovial cell populations, respectively. Representative platforms delivering antirheumatic drugs, glucocorticoids, natural products, nucleic acids, and functional nanomaterials are comparatively analyzed, while emerging targets including scavenger receptors, Fc gamma receptor I, pattern-recognition receptors, and integrin αvβ3 are discussed in their pathological contexts. Key translational issues, including receptor heterogeneity, target validation, formulation complexity, long-term safety, manufacturability, and patient stratification, are highlighted. Linking target biology with nanocarrier design may support more rational development of receptor-guided nanomedicines for RA.

articles.title: Mapping nanodelivery design for liver fibrosis: A mechanism-informed framework for functional integration.
articles.abstract: Liver fibrosis is sustained by interdependent hepatic stellate cell activation, inflammatory amplification, and gene-regulatory remodeling, yet nanodelivery platforms are commonly discussed by carrier class rather than by the functions required to address these disease mechanisms. This review develops a mechanism-function framework linking these pathological axes to six delivery functions: targeted delivery, drug stability, controlled release, bioavailability, biocompatibility, and immune evasion. After structured screening, formulation-level deduplication, supporting-information review, and independent verification, 124 eligible studies yielded 129 analytical units spanning HSC inactivation (n = 50), anti-inflammation (n = 33), and gene modulation (n = 46). Each unit was coded as directly demonstrated, assessed but not demonstrated, or not assessed/insufficiently reported for each function. The analysis identified modality-dependent integration patterns rather than a universal hierarchy. HSC-directed systems combined biocompatibility and targeted delivery with greater controlled-release integration; anti-inflammatory systems showed co-leading biocompatibility and targeted delivery, with TD-BC showing the highest raw co-occurrence and CR-BC the highest Jaccard similarity; and gene-modulation systems showed co-leading targeted delivery and biocompatibility reinforced by bioavailability. Direct evidence for drug stability and immune evasion remained comparatively sparse. All 30 core modality-level sensitivity comparisons preserved the top-two function sets and leading Jaccard pairs. BMS-986263 illustrates partial completion of the translational evidence chain: active-payload exposure and clinical tolerability were demonstrated, whereas cell-selective delivery, cargo integrity, release behavior, and immune-evasion performance were not directly established. These findings support an evidence-guided shift from maximal structural complexity toward mechanism-aligned, manufacturable platforms evaluated through active-payload exposure, target-compartment delivery, repeat-dose safety, and disease-stage-appropriate clinical design.

articles.title: The role of neurogenic inflammation and CGRP in migraine headache.
articles.abstract: The last 40 years have witnessed a thorough change in our understanding of the mechanisms underlying migraine, initiated by the discovery of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). A century ago, William Bayliss, Thomas Lewis and other pioneers introduced a visionary neurophysiological mechanism, brought about by peripheral terminals of a specialized subset of primary sensory neurons, which was named 'neurogenic inflammation'; in both mammal and human skin, action potentials generated by injured nerve terminals of primary sensory neurons can invade collateral fibres via antidromic conduction and release a mediator that 'produces the flare and enhances sensitivity of other sensory axons responsible for pain'. This mediator, much later identified as CGRP, provides the missing link between these early observations and modern therapeutic targets. Multiple monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor along with orally available small molecule antagonists of the CGRP receptor have revolutionized the prevention and acute treatment of migraine. The pharmacokinetic features of anti-CGRP drugs and the paracrine actions of CGRP suggest the proposal that the mechanism underlying migraine headache occurs in a spatially limited microenvironment located outside the blood-brain barrier. According to this hypothesis, the migraine headache milieu comprises CGRP-containing peripheral sensory nerve endings (C-fibre nociceptors) and neighbouring cells, including other nerve fibres (Aδ-fibres), vascular smooth muscle cells and Schwann cells wrapping these nerve fibres.

articles.title: Nursing interventions for managing treatment-related adverse effects of targeted anti-tumor therapies in adult cancer patients: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Targeted anti-tumor therapies, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, have improved clinical outcomes and survival across multiple cancers but are associated with clinically significant dermatologic, neurological, gastrointestinal, hematologic, and immune-related toxicities that compromise adherence and quality of life. OBJECTIVES: This scoping review aimed to systematically map the available evidence on nursing interventions used to prevent, monitor, and manage adverse effects associated with targeted anti-tumor therapies in adult cancer patients. METHODS: Eligible studies were English-language publications conducted between 2015 and 2025 that focused on nurse-led or nursing-centered interventions addressing the adverse effects of targeted anti-tumor therapies in adult oncology populations. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively by intervention type and adverse-effect domain. RESULTS: Of 742 records identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Study designs included two quasi-experimental studies and one randomized controlled trial protocol two cohort studies, seven narrative or integrative reviews, and two clinical practice guidelines. Five principal intervention categories were identified: patient education and self-management support; nurse-led oral targeted-drug management and continuity-of-care programs; home-based multidisciplinary interventions; telephone and telehealth-based toxicity monitoring; and symptom-specific supportive-care strategies. Across diverse settings, structured nursing interventions reduced toxicity burden, improved medication adherence, decreased unplanned healthcare use, and enhanced patient-reported quality of life and psychosocial outcomes. CONCLUSION: Nurse-led interventions may have an important and promising role in supporting the safe and effective use of targeted anti-tumor therapies in adults with cancer. Integrating structured education, continuity of care, multidisciplinary collaboration, and telehealth-enabled monitoring into routine oncology practice may optimize toxicity management and support treatment adherence. Further multicenter trials are needed to evaluate nursing protocols for antibody-drug conjugate-induced neuropathy and immune-related adverse events and to examine long-term clinical and economic outcomes. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://osf.io/5nvfe/identifier, 5nvfe.

articles.title: A systematic review on the possible role of microRNA-155 in cancer treatment.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Overexpression of microRNA-155 (miR-155) has been associated with cancer development, metastasis, and possible drug resistance. This systematic review analyzed the evidence from the existing literature on miR-155 expression in cancer patients undergoing treatment. METHODS: A thorough literature search was conducted in databases and search engines (ProQuest, PubMed, and Google Scholar) from January 2019 to December 2024 to identify clinical evidence on miR-155 expression in cancer treatments. To assess miR-155 expression in relation to clinical outcomes, we included 15 cancers in this systematic review. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, three independent reviewers selected, extracted, and assessed the data against the predefined inclusion criteria, and a fourth reviewer verified the assessments and resolved discrepancies. RESULTS: Of the 15 cancers analyzed, 19 eligible studies covering eight cancers were identified and included in the review, namely breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia, cutaneous melanoma, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, papillary thyroid cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Screening and evaluation of these 19 studies showed that miR-155 expression varied by cancer type, treatment strategy, and patient sample type. While most studies associated miR-155 overexpression with treatment resistance, a few reported an association between elevated miR-155 expression and enhanced treatment sensitivity. A limitation of this study is that the search for studies reporting miR-155 expression in relation to therapeutic outcomes in patients with cancer was restricted to three databases and a 5-year timeframe. CONCLUSION: Overall, the results of this study indicate that the prognostic and predictive significance of miR-155 warrants further evaluation. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO ID, CRD42025632573.

articles.title: FDA approves plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy for rare viral disease.
Dapagliflozin vs. Acetazolamide in Patients With Acute Heart Failure: A Randomized Controlled Trial (CHOICE-AHF).
articles.abstract: Early adjunctive therapies may improve decongestion and symptoms in acute heart failure. This trial compared dapagliflozin with acetazolamide when initiated early, focusing on dyspnea relief as the primary outcome and decongestive, diuretic, natriuretic, and safety outcomes. In this randomized, active-controlled trial, 108 adults hospitalized with acute heart failure, dyspnea, and objective evidence of congestion requiring intravenous loop diuretics were randomized to receive dapagliflozin 10 mg (N = 55) or acetazolamide 500 mg (N = 53) once daily for 3 days alongside standard care. The primary endpoint was the between-group difference in 72-hour dyspnea visual analog scale area under the curve. Secondary endpoints included successful decongestion within 3 days, diuretic and natriuretic responses, the relative change in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels from baseline to day 3, and safety. Acetazolamide produced a significantly lower 72-hour dyspnea area under the curve than dapagliflozin (2647.9 ± 1213.8 vs. 2988.7 ± 1196.7 mm × hour; P = 0.048). It increased cumulative urine output over 72 hours (12,200 vs. 10,000 mL; P = 0.019) and total natriuresis over 48 hours (824.7 vs. 547.9 mmol; P = 0.001). Dapagliflozin achieved a larger reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide at 72 hours (-34.2% vs. -25.0%; P = 0.003). Safety events were infrequent and similar. In conclusion, acetazolamide provided greater dyspnea relief, diuresis, and natriuresis, whereas dapagliflozin produced a larger short-term reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide. Further studies are needed to validate these findings. Trial registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06783166.

articles.title: Exploring lipid nanoparticle design spaces using self-regulating microfluidic machines and multiplexed in vivo biodistribution.
articles.abstract: Delivering therapeutic mRNA relies on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Finding optimal process parameters for new lipid combinations in LNP formulations remains a challenge. We used an automated, self-regulating microfluidic formulation platform developed for PEG-containing LNPs that actively changes process parameters to meet preset LNP diameters, and now explore how this automated production setup can be expanded to LNPs decorated with poly(2-oxazoline) (POx)-lipids. We also examine how the choice of lipopolymer affects the resulting physicochemical properties and in vivo biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. For that, we tested new LNPs by swapping poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipopolymers for alternatives based on poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (PMeOx) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx). For both POx-lipid variants, the platform independently identified optimal production conditions in four or fewer iterative cycles, yielding particles of the preset size and high mRNA encapsulation. Small-angle X-ray scattering revealed that smaller LNPs modified with PEtOx had greater structural surface variety and higher mRNA loading efficiency. When multiplexing these formulations in mice, the PEtOx-containing LNPs accumulated more in bone marrow and liver (and less in spleen and pancreas), compared to those with PEG, indicating trends that the chemistry of the lipopolymer affects the biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. By combining automated formulation and in vivo multiplexed testing, our approach provides a practical way to rapidly plan, formulate, and evaluate large pharmaceutical design spaces to select excipients and process parameters yielding optimal biological performance of LNPs.

articles.title: Reprogramming endocytic trafficking of antibody-drug conjugates to enhance tumor penetration and lysosomal delivery.
articles.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have transformed cancer treatment; however, challenges such as heterogeneous antigen expression and inefficient intracellular delivery continue to limit their clinical efficacy. Herein, we present a novel "signal-fusion" ADC strategy in which trafficking signal peptides were genetically fused to the C-terminus of trastuzumab (Tz), an anti-HER2 antibody. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed that these peptides remained solvent-exposed and structurally stable while positioned away from the antigen-binding regions. The resulting tetravalent signal-fusion constructs (T1/T2) enhanced endocytic trafficking by increasing receptor internalization and redirecting antibody complexes to lysosomes. Accordingly, T1 and T2 conjugated with vc-MMAF or vc-MMAE exhibited significantly enhanced cytotoxicity, improved tumor infiltration, and robust bystander effects across multiple cancer cell lines. Pharmacokinetic studies indicated plasma half-lives comparable to that of Tz, along with increased intratumoral accumulation. Furthermore, T1/T2-vc-MMAF induced prolonged tumor regression without observable toxicity in breast and gastric cancer models. Collectively, these findings highlight a promising approach for enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of next-generation ADCs.

articles.title: Long-resident ultrasmall zwitterionic nanoparticles normalize vessels and promote photosensitizer accumulation for enhanced photodynamic immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) holds promise for solid tumor treatment but is limited by its oxygen dependence and hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Vascular normalization improves perfusion and oxygenation, while the mismatch between the short normalization window and synchronous PDT impairs vascular function, aggravates hypoxia and blunts subsequent vascular normalization. Here, we develop ultra-small zwitterionic nanoparticles (RM-Ce6@St) based on the co-assembly of Ce6-grafted hyperbranched polycarbonates and oxalate ester-linked hyperbranched polycarbonates, encapsulating sunitinib to implement a "multiple accumulation and single irradiation" strategy for enhanced photodynamic immunotherapy. RM-Ce6@St, owing to the small-sized and zwitterionic surface features, exhibits significant tumor accumulation. Subsequently, the ROS-triggered release of sunitinib remodels the vasculature to enhance oxygenation, while long-retained Ce6 allows repeated dosing to cumulatively increase intratumoral Ce6 levels. Consequently, a single irradiation delivered within the normalization window enabled robust ROS generation and markedly improved PDT efficacy. In murine breast cancer models, a single irradiation within the normalization window achieved up to 90.7% tumor growth inhibition, compared with 40.3% for multiple irradiations prior to the window. This "multiple accumulation and single irradiation" further induced immunogenic cell death, promoted dendritic cell maturation, reduced myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration, resulting in potent control of primary and distant tumors.

articles.title: UBAP2L O-GlcNAcylation contributes to DDX21-associated stress granule formation and suppression of trophoblast pyroptosis in preeclampsia.
articles.abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a severe pregnancy disorder characterized by hypertension and multi-organ dysfunction. Impaired trophoblast function and defective spiral artery remodeling are considered the central pathological features of PE, leading to placental ischemia/hypoxia and a subsequent inflammatory cascade. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that pyroptosis contributes to placental dysfunction and the establishment of a pro-inflammatory microenvironment in PE; however, the mechanisms remain largely unclear. O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification is a reversible post-translational modification (PTM) that plays critical roles in maintaining cellular homeostasis and regulating multiple forms of programmed cell death (PCD), yet its role in pyroptosis during PE has not been elucidated. In the present study, we found that O-GlcNAcylation was markedly reduced in placental tissues from patients with PE and negatively correlated with pyroptosis. In both an LPS-induced PE-like mouse model and trophoblast cells, enhancement of O-GlcNAcylation significantly suppressed pyroptosis and ameliorated PE-like phenotypes. IP-MS identified UBAP2L as a critical O-GlcNAcylated protein. Mechanistically, T446, an O-GlcNAcylation site of UBAP2L, contributed to maintaining its protein stability by preventing ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation and promoted its interaction with DDX21, thereby promoting stress granule assembly. This process suppressed inflammasome activation and pyroptosis, improved trophoblast function, and ameliorated PE-like phenotypes. Collectively, our findings define an O-GlcNAcylation-UBAP2L-DDX21-stress granule-pyroptosis axis in PE and nominate O-GlcNAc signaling as a therapeutic target.

articles.title: Schistosomicidal potential of usnic acid: In vivo and in silico insights.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Schistosomiasis, caused by Schistosoma mansoni, remains a major public health concern worldwide. Praziquantel (PZQ) is currently the only drug available for treatment; however, it shows limited efficacy against immature stages of the parasite, highlighting the need for alternative therapeutic approaches. PURPOSE: In this , perspective, the present study aimed to evaluate the antischistosomal activity of usnic acid (UA) in a murine model, focusing on different developmental stages of the parasite, as well as to investigate its possible mechanisms of action through in silico approaches. METHODS: Infected mice were treated with UA at doses of 25 and 50 mg/kg, and parasitological parameters were assessed, including worm burden, intestinal and hepatic egg burden, oogram patterns, and numerical density of hepatic granulomas. Furthermore, molecular docking analyses were .performed using selected S. mansoni target proteins, along with predictions of pharmacokinetic and toxicological properties (ADMET). RESULTS: UA significantly reduced parasite burden, particularly in immature stages, reaching up to 85.59%, in contrast to the lower susceptibility of these stages to PZQ. Moreover, modulation of oviposition dynamics was observed, with a reduction of >60% in immature eggs and a significant increase of up to 53.8% in non-viable eggs, which was associated with a decrease in hepatic granuloma density. Docking analyses revealed that UA exhibits affinity for molecular targets involved in redox homeostasis and energy metabolism, including SmTGR and SmCA; ADMET predictions indicated a profile consistent with bioactive compounds, showing adequate intestinal absorption and tissue distribution, although with limitations related to permeability and potential toxicity. CONCLUSION: Overall, these findings suggest that UA exhibits relevant antischistosomal activity, with a possible multifactorial mechanism involving interference in parasite bioenergetics and redox balance. Its pronounced effect on immature stages highlights its potential as an alternative or adjunct therapy to PZQ; however, further studies are required to elucidate its mechanism of action and to comprehensively evaluate its safety profile.

articles.title: Tenascin‑C promotes pulmonary fibrosis via responding to oxidative stress and amplifying profibrotic signaling.
articles.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive and often fatal lung disease, and effective therapies remain limited, largely because its underlying pathogenic mechanisms are not fully understood. Here, we investigated the stage-specific role of the extracellular matrix protein Tenascin-C (TNC) in pulmonary fibrogenesis. Analysis of four independent human transcriptomic datasets identified 195 differentially expressed genes shared across datasets, among which TNC was markedly upregulated and functionally enriched in fibrosis- and matrix-associated pathways. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis indicated that TNC expression was primarily detected in fibroblasts and was associated with fibrotic differentiation. Experiments in mice with bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis further confirmed progressive TNC upregulation and demonstrated its colocalization with α-SMA+ myofibroblasts. Functionally, TNC deficiency inhibited fibroblast proliferation, migration, and activation in vitro and significantly improved survival and attenuated collagen deposition and fibrotic damage in vivo. Notably, TNC exhibited a temporal functional switch during disease progression. During the early inflammatory phase, TNC responded to oxidative stress and promoted the recruitment of CD68+ macrophages, thereby accelerating inflammatory infiltration. This effect was further confirmed in fibroblast-macrophage co-cultures treated with H2O2. During the late fibrotic phase, TNC amplified the fibrotic cascade by enhancing TGF-β-driven fibroblast activation and increasing α-SMA and collagen I expression. Overall, our findings establish TNC as a key spatiotemporal hub linking the oxidative stress-inflammation-fibrosis cascade, making it a promising therapeutic target for pulmonary fibrosis.

articles.title: Ginsenoside Rg6 ameliorates COPD by targeting RAGE to suppress MAPK/NF-κB signaling, thereby preserving alveolar barrier integrity and attenuating EMT.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is pathologically characterized by progressive alveolar epithelial barrier disruption, a pathological process primarily driven by chronic cigarette smoke exposure. While Ginsenoside Rg6 (Rg6) has shown therapeutic promise in pulmonary injury models, its direct molecular targets and the precise mechanisms by which it preserves barrier integrity remain unclear. PURPOSE: This study investigates whether Rg6 mitigates COPD by directly targeting the RAGE receptor, thereby suppressing the downstream signaling axes concurrently preserve alveolar barrier integrity and attenuate epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). METHODS: The therapeutic efficacy of Rg6 was evaluated in CSE-challenged MLE-12 alveolar epithelial cells and an LPS/CS-driven mouse COPD model. Transcriptomic profiling was utilized to identify upstream regulatory nodes. Direct Rg6-RAGE engagement was rigorously validated via molecular docking, MD simulations, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), DARTS, and CETSA. The functional dependency of Rg6's protective effects on RAGE was dissected using siRNA knockdown in vitro and AAV-shRAGE delivery in vivo. RESULTS: Oral Rg6 significantly ameliorated pulmonary function decline, emphysema, and the inflammatory microenvironment in COPD mice, achieving efficacy comparable to dexamethasone. Crucially, Rg6 effectively preserved alveolar barrier integrity, restored tight junctions, and attenuated EMT-associated phenotypic shifts. Transcriptomic profiling identified the AGE-RAGE axis as the central upstream hub governing this structural protection. Comprehensive biophysical assays confirmed that Rg6 directly binds to and thermodynamically stabilizes the RAGE protein pocket. Mechanistically, Rg6 suppressed RAGE-mediated hyperactivation of the MAPK (p38, JNK) and NF-κB (p65) cascades, which serve as the central drivers for tight junction disassembly and EMT in epithelial cells. Furthermore, RAGE ablation in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that Rg6's capacity to preserve epithelial architecture is primarily RAGE-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: Rg6 directly targets alveolar RAGE to inhibit the RAGE-MAPK/NF-κB signaling cascade. By suppressing this axis, Rg6 concurrently preserves alveolar barrier integrity and attenuates EMT-like transitions, actively restoring alveolar structural homeostasis and positioning it as a promising therapeutic candidate for COPD.

articles.title: Atractylenolide III alleviates MASLD by inhibiting lipid synthesis and apoptosis via PTEN.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as a major global health issue. This study aims to investigate the ameliorative effects of atractylenolide III (ATL III) on MASLD and its underlying molecular mechanisms, thereby providing theoretical basis and experimental support for the development of therapeutic drugs for MASLD. METHODS: A high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mouse model and a combination of oleic acid and palmitic acid (PO)-induced lipid deposition model in AML-12 hepatocytes were established. The therapeutic effects of ATL III on hepatic lipid accumulation, injury, and inflammation were evaluated using biochemical assays, histopathological staining, immunofluorescence, Western blot (WB), and quantitative real-time PCR. Transcriptome sequencing was performed to screen for key targets, and molecular docking together with cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were used to validate the potential binding between ATL III and the target protein. The findings were further verified using a liver-specific Pten knockdown mouse model. RESULTS: In vivo experiments showed that ATL III significantly ameliorated hepatic lipid accumulation, injury, and inflammatory response in HFD feeding mice. In vitro experiments demonstrated that ATL III effectively reduced lipid accumulation in PO-induced AML-12 cells without affecting cell viability. Transcriptome sequencing and KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes regulated by ATL III were enriched in the phosphatidylinositol 3‑kinase (PI3K)/serine/threonine protein kinase B (AKT), fatty acid metabolism, and apoptosis pathways. Further studies showed that ATL III engaged PTEN in a cellular context and upregulated its expression, thereby inhibiting excessive AKT activation. WB analysis confirmed that ATL III regulated lipid synthesis and apoptosis-related proteins via the PTEN/AKT axis. Notably, liver‑specific knockdown of Pten significantly attenuated the ameliorative effects of ATL III on the expression of the above molecules, as well as on liver injury and lipid accumulation. CONCLUSIONS: ATL III ameliorates hepatic steatosis, injury, and inflammation in HFD-induced MASLD mice. Mechanistically, ATL III upregulates PTEN expression and suppresses excessive AKT activation, thereby reducing hepatic lipid synthesis and hepatocyte apoptosis. Liver-specific knockdown of Pten attenuates the protective effects of ATL III, confirming that PTEN is functionally required for its beneficial actions. These findings suggest that ATL III represents a potential therapeutic candidate for MASLD by acting through the PTEN/AKT pathway.

articles.title: Qili Qiangxin capsule as adjunctive therapy for heart failure after acute myocardial infarction: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Heart failure (HF) after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality despite advances in conventional therapy. Qili Qiangxin Capsule (QLQX) has been widely used as an adjunctive treatment for HF in China, but its efficacy and safety in patients with HF after AMI require further evaluation. METHODS: Seven databases were searched from their inception to January 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing QLQX plus conventional Western medicine (WM) with WM alone were included. The primary outcome was N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP). Secondary outcomes included left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD), left ventricular end-systolic diameter (LVESD), left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), clinical response rate, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), quality of life, all-cause mortality, heart failure-related hospitalisation, and adverse events. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4. RESULTS: A total of 16 RCTs involving 1391 participants were included. Compared with WM alone, QLQX plus WM was associated with greater reductions in NT-proBNP, BNP, LVEDD, LVESD, and hs-CRP, and improving LVEF, quality of life and the clinical response rate. No statistical differences were observed in LVEDV, all-cause mortality, and adverse events. Heart failure-related hospitalisation was not reported in any included study. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as low or very low according to the GRADE approach. CONCLUSION: QLQX plus conventional WM was associated with improvements in several surrogate and short-term clinical outcomes in patients with HF after AMI. However, the certainty of evidence was low or very low, and data on mortality and heart failure-related hospitalisation were insufficient. The current evidence is therefore inadequate to determine whether QLQX improves long-term clinical prognosis. Further high-quality RCTs with longer follow-up and clinically important endpoints are needed. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261277047, identifier CRD420261277047.

articles.title: Adjunctive probiotics may reduce adverse events during vonoprazan-based Helicobacter pylori eradication: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vonoprazan is pharmacologically distinct from proton pump inhibitors and is increasingly incorporated into Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens. Previous meta-analyses of probiotic adjuncts pooled heterogeneous acid-suppressive agents, antibiotic backbones, probiotic products, and treatment durations, limiting inference about the incremental effect of probiotics when the vonoprazan-based regimen is otherwise fixed. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether adjunctive probiotics improve tolerability and eradication outcomes when randomized groups receive an otherwise identical vonoprazan-based H. pylori regimen. METHODS: We searched eight bibliographic databases and three trial registries from inception through 15 July 2026. Eligible studies were randomized trials in adults comparing an identical vonoprazan-based regimen with or without concurrently administered probiotics. Risk ratios were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. We also reported 95% prediction intervals, absolute effects, outcome-specific RoB 2 assessments, sensitivity analyses, and GRADE certainty ratings. RESULTS: Nine studies involving 1,270 participants were included. Adjunctive probiotics reduced overall adverse events (5 studies, 611 participants; RR = 0.30, 95%CI: 0.17-0.53; P = 0.004; I2 = 0%; 95% prediction interval: 0.12-0.79), corresponding to 182 fewer affected participants per 1,000 treated (moderate-certainty evidence). Intention-to-treat eradication was slightly higher with probiotics (7 studies, 910 participants; RR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.00-1.19; I2 = 47.8%), but the prediction interval crossed the null and sensitivity analyses were not statistically significant. Per-protocol eradication showed little or no difference (5 studies, 698 participants; RR = 1.03, 95%CI: 0.97-1.09), and good adherence was not clearly improved. CONCLUSION: Among Chinese adults, adjunctive probiotics probably reduce overall adverse events during vonoprazan-based H. pylori eradication therapy. The available evidence does not establish a reliable improvement in eradication success, and applicability to populations outside China remains uncertain. PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD420261450405.

articles.title: Crossing subfamily borders: Mechanosensitive TREK-1 and alkaline-activated TASK-4 form heterodimers with unique functional and pharmacological properties.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The tandem of two-pore-domain potassium (K2P) channels TREK-1 and TASK-4 are expressed in the heart and pancreatic beta-cells. As TREK-1 and TASK-4 belong to distinct subfamilies with different functional hallmarks, heteromerization of these two channels was highly unexpected. However, due to their shared expression in these tissues and their involvement in congenital cardiac arrhythmias, the aim of this study was to probe for a possible formation of TREK-1/TASK-4 heterodimers. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Two-electrode voltage-clamp and inside-out macropatch clamp recordings, together with immunohistochemistry and chemiluminescence-based ELISA assays, were utilized to describe heteromerization of TREK-1 and TASK-4 channels and elucidate the characteristics of this heteromeric channel complex. KEY RESULTS: Here, we show that the mechanosensitive TREK-1 forms heteromeric channel complexes with the alkaline-activated TASK-4. The resulting heterodimers of these only remotely related channels have an enhanced temperature sensitivity, an altered pH dependence and regulation by extracellular sodium. Unlike TREK-1, heteromeric TREK-1/TASK-4 channels are not inhibited via Gs-coupled receptor activation, as the heterodimeric channels are not PKA sensitive. Strikingly, these novel heterodimeric channel complexes are characterized by a unique pharmacology. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: The newly described heterodimerization across different K2P channel families is of major relevance for drugs targeting TASK-4 or TREK-1. Their functional co-expression in different tissues raises the possibility of developing drugs against cardiac arrhythmias and Type 2 diabetes by specifically targeting these unique heterodimeric channel complexes.

articles.title: RETRACTION: Exploring the Antidepressant Potential of Yueju Pill: Insights from Traditional Chinese Medicine.
Clinical Pharmacology in Transgender Medicine: What Gaps Remain?
articles.abstract: Mechanistic information is limited about the effects of gender-affirming hormone therapy and the unique factors that influence the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion properties of medications across therapeutic classes for transgender people. Opportunities exist to address knowledge gaps in transgender medicine using well-designed probe substrate studies, endogenous biomarkers of drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters, and real-world data to identify and address factors that contribute to interindividual variability in drug disposition for transgender people across the life course.

articles.title: PPARγ signaling pathway: strategies and limitations of natural compounds in the treatment of ulcerative colitis.
articles.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterized by persistent inflammatory activation, immune dysregulation, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and damage to the mucosal barrier. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is a key nuclear receptor involved in maintaining intestinal immunity and mucosal homeostasis. Reduced PPARγ expression or impaired function may weaken its negative regulatory role in pro-inflammatory signaling and disrupt the Th17/Treg balance, macrophage polarization, gut microbiota homeostasis, and barrier integrity, making PPARγ a crucial molecular hub linking multiple pathological processes in UC. Due to their structural diversity and multi-target regulatory properties, natural compounds are attracting increasing attention as potential modulators of PPARγ-related networks. This review systematically summarizes the current preclinical evidence regarding natural compounds that target PPARγ and its associated signaling networks in UC, with particular emphasis on their roles in regulating inflammatory responses, immune cell function, the Th17/Treg balance, the gut microbiota, and mucosal barrier integrity through PPARγ-related pathways (including AMPK, NF-κB, mTOR, SIRT1, MAPK, Nrf2, and STAT). Importantly, the currently available evidence primarily stems from in vitro cellular and in vivo animal studies; therefore, it mainly provides mechanistic and preclinical support rather than evidence of clinical efficacy. Current research is also limited by insufficient evaluation of specific targets, reliance on a limited range of disease models, and inadequate characterization of pharmacokinetic and safety profiles. Future research should prioritize rigorous evaluation of PPARγ-dependent mechanisms, conduct pharmacokinetic and safety assessments, and design rigorous human studies and clinical trials to establish the therapeutic potential of these natural compounds in UC. This review provides a framework for critically evaluating the existing evidence and guiding the development and evaluation of PPARγ-targeting natural compounds for UC.

articles.title: Treatment of vascular dementia based on neuroprotection and neural repair strategies: from pathophysiology to natural products.
articles.abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a heterogeneous cognitive disorder associated with cerebrovascular pathology and persistent vascular dysfunction. Because effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited, natural products have attracted interest as potential interventions for the complex pathology of VaD. This review examines their effects from two complementary perspectives: neuroprotection and neural repair. Experimental studies indicate that natural products can influence several interconnected processes, including redox imbalance, neuroinflammation, cell survival, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, vascular remodeling, neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity. However, the available evidence varies considerably among isolated compounds, botanical extracts, and herbal formulations. Some isolated compounds have been supported by relatively coherent relationships between molecular targets, tissue responses, and functional outcomes, whereas evidence from clinical studies remains much more limited. We therefore consider the current mechanistic evidence together with the major challenges in pharmacokinetics, quality control, and clinical translation.

articles.title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome subphenotypes: the translational path from pathobiology to precision medicine.
articles.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a highly heterogeneous critical illness syndrome lacking effective targeted therapies, partly due to the diverse patient population. Subphenotype research aims to identify homogeneous patient subgroups sharing common biological, physiological, or clinical characteristics, enabling prognostic and predictive enrichment. This review systematically summarizes current ARDS subphenotype research, from pathobiological mechanisms to multidimensional identification based on etiology, imaging, biomarkers, respiratory mechanics, and transcriptomics. We highlight evidence for differential prognoses and treatment responses across subphenotypes, including variable effects of neuromuscular blockade, corticosteroids, and prone positioning. We further discuss challenges and future directions in translating subphenotype classification into bedside practice. This article provides a theoretical framework and practical guidance for advancing precision medicine in ARDS.

articles.title: Availability of age-stratified evidence for GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors: an analysis of European public assessment reports with a focus on older patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors are widely prescribed and their use is increasingly frequent in older patient populations. We evaluated the extent to which older patients were represented in clinical trials of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. METHODS: To identify relevant trials, we screened the respective European Public Assessment Reports (n = 28) and the European Summaries of Product Characteristics (n = 9) for each of the six approved medicines. Further information was retrieved from the original publications of the identified trials and from the ClinicalTrials.gov database (n = 40). Overall, we analyzed n = 185 sources for 106 trial populations. RESULTS: For 46% of the 106 analyzed trial populations, data for patients ≥65 years were identified. Where age distributions were reported, patients aged 75 years or older were markedly underrepresented in nearly all trials, and subgroup analyses of efficacy and safety by age were rarely published. Especially in cardiovascular outcome trials and trials including patients with chronic kidney disease or chronic heart failure, older patients were better represented and analyses of primary outcomes in different age groups were published more frequently. Safety data on different age groups were mainly identified in the European Public Assessment Reports. Whereas increasing numbers of adverse events with older age were observed in several trials, this increase typically affected all trial arms, independent of the drug treatment. CONCLUSION: Data availability for patients with older age is insufficient from pivotal trials to properly describe efficacy or safety of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin.

articles.title: Subcutaneous drug delivery: from simple release testing to biomimetic systems.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Subcutaneous (SC) administration is increasingly used for biologics and long-acting therapeutics, yet formulation performance and human bioavailability remain difficult to predict. This is because the injection site is a heterogenous environment comprising extracellular matrix, interstitial fluid, tissue-resident cells, and distinct vascular and lymphatic vessels. AREAS COVERED: This review evaluates 17-year SC drug-delivery growth, market trends, and in vitro tools spanning shake-flask, dialysis, USP apparatus 4, and biomimetic acellular platforms including SCISSOR, BioJect, ESCAR, and hydrogel-based membrane-inserts. Cellular and microphysiological systems, including 3D adipose models, SubCuTIS, and lymphatics-on-chip, are assessed alongside in silico approaches. Peer-reviewed studies and industry and regulatory reports are evaluated for physiological relevance, accessibility, validation, and translational utility. EXPERT OPINION: Progress has been substantial, but no current model independently reproduces the mechanisms governing human SC absorption. Cellular components remain underutilized despite extensive foundational work in related fields. Priorities include physiologically characterized matrices, realistic interstitial fluids, quantitative mass-balance endpoints, and multicenter validation against human pharmacokinetic data. A modular, fit-for-purpose qualification strategy offers the most practical route toward predictive and animal-sparing SC drug development.

articles.title: Glycol chitosan thermogels: a versatile platform for advanced drug delivery.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Injectable thermogels are promising localized drug delivery platforms as their temperature-triggered in situ gelation facilitates practical administration. However, conventional systems suffer from high critical gelation concentrations, limited biodegradability, cytotoxicity, or acidic degradation, which can cause local inflammation. Glycol chitosan (GC)-based thermogels have emerged as a promising alternative, combining aqueous solubility at physiological pH, biodegradability, biocompatibility, mucoadhesion, low-concentration gelation, and structural versatility. AREAS COVERED: This review comprehensively examines GC-based thermogels, highlighting how hydrophobic modifications govern their structure-property relationships and thermo-responsive gelation. It evaluates their performance as localized reservoirs for small-molecule drugs, biomacromolecules, and genes across challenging anatomical sites with rapid physiological clearance, including ocular, inner ear, and vaginal sites, while summarizing emerging biofunctional applications in cell delivery, wound healing, and 3D biofabrication. Recent advances in prodrug thermogels, dual crosslinked networks, and biohybrid formulations are also discussed. EXPERT OPINION: To advance GC-based thermogels toward clinical implementation, formulation design must prioritize controlled degradation synchronized with payload release and therapeutic duration. Translation will require standardized polymer characterization, reproducible and scalable manufacturing, sterilization-compatible processing, long-term local safety assessment, and rigorous benchmarking in clinically relevant models. Ultimately, indication-specific formulations with functionality tailored to defined therapeutic needs are more likely to achieve clinical translation than a universal platform approach.

articles.title: Inappropriate prescribing of gastric acid suppressants: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: AIM: Inappropriate prescribing of gastric acid suppressants (GASs) may compromise treatment outcomes. This study aimed to examine the prevalence of inappropriate prescribing of GASs in all healthcare settings. METHODS: This PROSPERO-registered systematic literature review used PubMed and Embase databases to identify original English-language studies published between 1 January 2000 and 15 December 2025. Studies reporting the number of inappropriate GASs prescribing among patients receiving GASs were included. EndNote, Rayyan and ASReview were used to select studies. RESULTS: Overall, 141 studies from 44 countries were included. The number of patients in the studies ranged from 36 to 922 436. The pooled prevalence of inappropriate prescribing for all continents was 53% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 49% to 57%), prediction interval 15% to 89%, I2 = 99.9% and τ2 = 0.92. Doi plots of the publication bias analysis showed asymmetry in some models (Luis Furuya-Kanamori index = -4.48), but the Copas-adjusted estimate for the overall dataset was essentially identical to the unadjusted pooled estimate, indicating that although small-study effects may be present, publication bias is unlikely to affect the overall pooled prevalence. Based on our dataset, we selected several moderators to evaluate. From the selected moderators, we found that the study setting was the factor significantly associated with differences in the pooled prevalence (P = 0.02). CONCLUSION: Across published studies, approximately half of prescribed GASs was classified as inappropriate. This result highlights the global need for healthcare providers to effectively prevent and discontinue the inappropriate prescribing of GASs.

articles.title: Medicinal Plants and Fungi of the Sikkim Himalaya for Hypertension and Cardiovascular Disorders: Ethnopharmacology, Mechanisms, and Cardiovascular Relevance.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of global mortality, driven by mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, and dysregulated cellular signaling. Despite extensive use of plant-based therapies for circulatory disorders, many ethnomedicinal claims lack molecular validation. In the biodiversity-rich Sikkim Himalaya, India, traditional medicinal plant use by Lepcha, Bhutia, and Nepali communities remains unsystematically integrated with cardiovascular evidence, with limited classification into three evidence tiers: Tier I (mechanistically validated), Tier II (mechanistically suggestive), and Tier III (pharmacologically divergent). AIM OF THE STUDY: To critically assess the extent to which the traditional cardiovascular uses of medicinal plants and fungi from the Sikkim Himalaya, India, are supported by experimental pharmacological and molecular evidence, and to classify the available evidence according to its mechanistic strength. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A PRISMA 2020-guided narrative review was conducted to identify, screen, and report the available literature using predefined procedures. The retrieved evidence was synthesized qualitatively to integrate ethnopharmacological, pharmacological, phytochemical, and molecular mechanistic findings. Literature from Jan 1950 to March 2026 was retrieved from PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar. Studies were screened using predefined inclusion criteria focusing on Sikkim-based ethnomedicinal use and cardiovascular indications. Data were extracted on species identity, traditional use, phytochemistry, and molecular mechanisms, followed by qualitative synthesis. RESULTS: Fifteen medicinal plant and fungal taxa were identified. Five taxa, including Rhododendron arboreum Sm., Centella asiatica (L.) Urb., Nardostachys jatamansi (D.Don) DC., Oroxylum indicum (L.) Kurz, and Ophiocordyceps sinensis (Berk.) G.H.Sung, J.M.Sung, Hywel-Jones & Spatafora, demonstrated cardioprotective effects in myocardial injury models via modulation of mitochondrial stability, inflammatory signaling, and PI3K/Akt and AMPK pathways. Evidence was stratified into three tiers: Tier I, mechanistically validated; Tier II, mechanistically suggestive; and Tier III, pharmacologically divergent. CONCLUSIONS: Stress-adaptive Himalayan phytochemistry converges with conserved cardiovascular signaling pathways, supporting their potential as candidates for further preclinical cardiovascular investigation. However, integration of metabolomics, pharmacokinetics, disease-relevant models, and clinical studies is required to establish therapeutic efficacy and enable clinical translation.

articles.title: Born to have obesity: rodent experimental models to study childhood obesity.
articles.abstract: Childhood obesity is a complex and rapidly growing global health challenge, associated with early-onset metabolic disturbances and increased risk of cardiometabolic and endocrine disorders in later life. Its development reflects the interplay of genetic predisposition, early-life environmental exposures, dietary and physical activity patterns, and psychosocial influences. Compared to adults, children exhibit distinct patterns of fat distribution, hormonal regulation, and metabolic responses, highlighting the need for research approaches tailored to pediatric populations. Early-life metabolic programming, including epigenetic modifications and alterations in adipose tissue development, plays a central role in determining long-term susceptibility to obesity and related comorbidities, such as insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and cardiovascular disease. Translational animal models, particularly mice, provide essential tools to investigate these mechanisms under controlled conditions, offering advantages including genetic tractability, short lifespan, and conserved metabolic pathways. However, differences in physiology and environmental context limit the direct extrapolation to humans. This review critically compares genetic, dietary, and early-life overnutrition models according to developmental timing, experimental objectives, and translational limitations. Particular emphasis is placed on model-selection strategies for investigating metabolic programming, pediatric obesity-related complications, and therapeutic responses, with the aim of guiding the design of more reproducible and clinically relevant preclinical studies.

articles.title: Rational design of inhaled antibacterials targeting alveolar macrophages for efficient killing of resistant bacteria associated with lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs).
articles.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria, are a leading cause of global death and morbidity. One of the principal limitations in treating respiratory bacterial infections is inefficient delivery and appropriate therapeutic drug concentrations to infected cells, as required to kill resistant bacteria. Inhaled antibiotic delivery technology specifically delivers antibacterials directly into the infected cells of the lungs and provides the required therapeutic concentration at a very low delivered dose, with a greatly reduced risk of systemic adverse effects. An alveolar macrophage (AM)-targeted antibiotic delivery strategy utilizing receptor-ligand interactions or stimuli-responsive mechanisms of drug release demonstrated efficient killing of intracellular bacteria. The rational design of antibacterials or formulations for inhalation is the key to achieving this goal. Based on ligand chemistry, decorating antibiotic carriers with ligands that target specific AM receptors is a novel strategy to ensure precise antibiotic delivery to the site of infection while reducing both the side effects associated with high systemic doses and the risk of further promoting antibiotic resistance. This review highlights advances in AM-targeted inhaled antibacterials, identification of appropriate ligands for specific AM receptors, mechanisms of interaction, and subsequent release of antibiotics through carrier degradation, pH-responsive behavior, or enzymatic cleavage to eradicate resistant bacteria. Finally, we discuss the ongoing challenges and future directions for AM-targeted inhaled antibacterials against LRTIs.

articles.title: Concentration categories do not represent equivalent exposure intensity in comparative PFAS transcriptomics.
articles.abstract: Sprenger et al. (2026) provide an extensive transcriptomic dataset covering 33 PFAS congeners in differentiated HepaRG cells and report broadly comparable molecular responses across structurally diverse substances. The dataset is valuable, but the cross-PFAS comparison requires a clearer distinction between relative concentration categories, numerical exposure concentrations and toxicological potency. For each PFAS, three non-cytotoxic concentrations were selected individually. The resulting numerical concentrations ranged from 5 to 250 µM. All 33 congeners were tested at 25 µM, 25 of 33 at 100 µM and 22 of 33 at 250 µM. Nevertheless, the subsequent comparative IPA analyses were based on the labels "low", "medium" and "high", rather than numerical concentrations. These labels therefore do not represent equivalent exposure intensities across PFAS. The distinction becomes consequential because the authors report concentration-dependent increases in differentially expressed genes for most compounds and because several additional pathways emerged predominantly at the high concentration, which was close to the cytotoxicity threshold for some PFAS but substantially below it for others. Thus, the high category can simultaneously encode chemical identity, nominal dose and position relative to cytotoxicity. This does not mean that category-based comparisons are invalid. Rather, they answer a narrower question: whether compounds perturb common pathways at their individually selected exposure levels. Concentration-resolved or potency-based analyses would complement this approach and help distinguish shared molecular response from comparable potency and from effects emerging only at different positions on the concentration-response continuum.

articles.title: The role of pharmacotherapy in improving quality of life among patients with MAFLD: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical studies confirm that patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) commonly experience a significant decline in quality of life (QOL). However, existing research findings on the efficacy of drug therapies in improving their QOL remain inconsistent, and quantitative evidence from meta-analyses is lacking. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effectiveness of drug therapy in improving the QOL of patients with MAFLD. METHODS: We systematically searched four electronic databases from their inception to 24 October 2025. All statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager software (version 5.4). RESULTS: The meta-analysis revealed that drug intervention had a positive effect only on the Physical Component Summary (PCS) score (SMD: 0.19, 95% CI: 0.05-0.34, I2 = 0, p-heterogeneity = 0.45). Subgroup analysis indicated that the ≤12-month drug intervention group demonstrated improvement in the Physical Component Summary score (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.03-0.46, I2 = 0, p-heterogeneity = 0.26). CONCLUSION: Moderate to very low-quality evidence indicates that pharmacological interventions yield a small, statistically significant improvement in the SF-36 PCS score in MAFLD patients, but this change does not meet the established minimal clinically important difference threshold for this population. To better elucidate the full impact of medications on patients' QOL, future studies should prioritize comprehensive, multidimensional assessments of patient-reported outcomes, while remaining focused on hepatic pathology.

articles.title: Neuroinflammation: an important mechanism of sevoflurane-induced developmental neurotoxicity.
articles.abstract: For more than 150 years, the effects of general anaesthetics were assumed to be transient and harmless. However, in the last 2 decades, an increasing number of studies have reported structural and cognitive problems in the brain, particularly the developing brain. Despite increasing evidence of anaesthetic-induced neurotoxicity in animal research, data in humans have been contradictory and confusing. Sevoflurane is the most often used anaesthetic in newborns and applied during millions of procedures worldwide each year; however, this medicine has the potential to be neurotoxic. Short-term or a single exposure to sevoflurane has little effect on cognitive function; however, lengthy or repetitive exposure to general anaesthetics can result in cognitive impairment. This review focuses on the processes through which sevoflurane exposure during development can cause long-term negative consequences for the brain. We focus extensively on the link between sevoflurane anaesthesia and neuroinflammation as critical pathways for sevoflurane-induced developmental neurotoxicity. These findings are intended to offer a theoretical framework for the development of precise neuroprotective techniques and the optimization of current anaesthetic regimens.

articles.title: Adverse effects of FDA-approved RNA therapeutics: a cross-platform analysis of RNA design, delivery systems, and safety profiles.
articles.abstract: RNA therapeutics have emerged as a promising and effective tool to treat a wide range of genetic, metabolic, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases by directly modulating the gene expression or directing transient protein production. Currently, more than 20 RNA-based drugs have been approved by the FDA, and due to their recent introduction into the clinical practice, long-term safety data remain limited and comparisons of adverse effects across platforms are lacking. This review focuses on the three major RNA therapeutic platforms, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNA (siRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) and intends to provide a cross-platform analysis of their adverse effects. We searched studies published up to June 2026 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using terms related to RNA therapeutics, individual drug names, safety and toxicity outcomes. Clinical trials, extension studies, pharmacovigilance reports, regulatory documents, and prescribing information were considered for each FDA-approved ASO, siRNA and mRNA agent. The observed safety profiles are associated with an interaction between RNA modality and additional determinants, including chemical modification, delivery system, route of administration, biodistribution, target tissue, and clinical context. Innate immune activation represents a potential shared mechanism, whereas sequence-dependent off-target effects, delivery-associated reactions, administration-related complications, and organ-specific toxicities differ in relevance and mechanism among ASO, siRNA, and mRNA therapeutics. Although most reported adverse effects are mild to moderate, important research gaps regarding long-term safety, pediatric use and rare adverse effects still exist, underscoring the need for further optimization of RNA drug design and delivery technologies, as well as continued pharmacovigilance.

articles.title: Integrating the gut microbiome into therapeutic drug monitoring and model-informed precision dosing: a clinical pharmacy perspective.
articles.abstract: Interindividual variability in drug response remains a central obstacle to effective pharmacotherapy, and much of it persists after accounting for the pharmacogenomic factors that currently guide individualized treatment. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) and model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) have become a mature, covariate-driven discipline that tailors dose to renal function, body size, age, and genotype, yet one determinant of drug exposure is conspicuously absent from these frameworks: the gut microbiome. Although gut bacteria are now known to alter the pharmacokinetics of many drugs, microbial variation is not represented in dosing models and is instead absorbed into unexplained residual variability. This review reframes the gut microbiome as a measurable, dosing-relevant covariate rather than a mechanistic phenomenon. We organize the mechanisms by which gut bacteria shape drug pharmacokinetics into four classes (biotransformation, inactivation, bioaccumulation, and indirect modulation of host enzymes and enterohepatic recirculation) and summarize the landmark evidence that microbial variation produces measurable interindividual differences in exposure and response, graded explicitly by evidential tier so that causal and associative findings are not conflated. We then locate the microbiome blind spot within current TDM and MIPD, and propose an operational framework specifying what microbial features to measure, how they should be sampled and measured reproducibly, and how to integrate them into population-pharmacokinetic, Bayesian, machine-learning, and physiologically based dosing models, setting out for each route its data requirements, validation strategy, limitations, and current prototyping status, and illustrating the framework with three worked examples of differing evidential maturity. Finally, we translate the framework into strategies actionable by clinical pharmacists and delineate the biological, methodological, and translational obstacles ahead, including the workflow burden, cost, and biomarker-qualification requirements that adoption would entail. By treating the microbiome as a covariate, this perspective charts a route toward microbiome-informed precision dosing at the bedside.

articles.title: Therapeutic effects and mechanisms of neutrophil membrane-coated MXene (Ti 3 C 2 T x ) nanoparticles for sepsis treatment.
articles.abstract: Sepsis, a life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated infection response, remains a high-mortality global health burden characterized by the systemic overproduction of pro-inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Timely anti-infective/anti-inflammatory interventions in the early onset window drastically improve sepsis prognosis, yet current therapeutic efficacy remains severely constrained by the global antibiotic resistance crisis. As a two-dimensional nanomaterial, Ti3C2Tx MXene displays potent intrinsic antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities. We herein engineer a neutrophil membrane-coated Ti3C2Tx nanoplatform (NM@Ti3C2Tx NPs) for targeted sepsis therapy. Experimental validation confirms this formulation mitigates sepsis-triggered oxidative stress injury via synergistic antioxidant pathways, with favorable colloidal stability and confirmed in vitro biocompatibility. In CLP-induced murine sepsis models, it attenuates systemic pro-inflammatory cascades, alleviates hypothermia and multi-organ damage, and improves survival. Collectively, this multifunctional platform integrating targeted antibacterial action and oxidative stress modulation presents a promising candidate for sepsis translational therapy.

articles.title: Exploration of various administration routes for the nitric oxide donating organic nitrite, nitrosooxypropanol, in a porcine model.
articles.abstract: Organic nitrites are restricted to intravenous or inhaled administration. The aim was to explore novel administration routes for an organic nitrite, previously demonstrated to have pulmonary selectivity, in normal and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Hemodynamic and respiratory variables, including fraction of exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), were measured in 13 anesthetized pigs. In naïve conditions, nitrosooxypropanol (PDNO) was given subcutaneously (100-1600 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose, 30 min interval), intramuscularly (50-400 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose, 30 min interval), intravenously (5-80 nmol/kg/min; 30 min infusion), intranasally (500-2000 nmol/kg boli), and sublingually (80-16,240 nmol/kg boli). In pulmonary hypertension (intravenous infusion of U46619), PDNO was given intravenously (5-45 nmol/kg/min; 15-20 mins infusion/dose) and subcutaneously (200-1800 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose at 20 min interval). Recovery was calculated using FeNO. PDNO, given by all administration routes, dose-dependently decreased systemic blood pressure and increased FeNO. Subcutaneous and intramuscular administration induced slow-onset (9 min to maximum effect) and long-lasting effects (~30 min). Intravenous administration induced rapid effects (1-2 min to steady state) and prompt decline after infusion cessation. The proportion of PDNO reaching exhaled gas (intravenous administration as reference; FeNO-based recovery) was 17% (intramuscularly) and 9% (subcutaneously). In pulmonary hypertension, intravenous and subcutaneous administration decreased the pulmonary/systemic vascular resistance-ratio. In this exploratory proof-of-concept study evaluating novel administration routes for organic nitrites, PDNO demonstrated measurable biological effects and acceptable FeNO-based recovery following intramuscular and subcutaneous administration. Furthermore, intranasal and tentatively sublingual administration showed biological effects. Future work on formulation and investigations into relevant disease models is warranted.

articles.title: Hepa-SENS: ASGPR-mediated hepatocyte delivery and attenuated unwanted immune recognition for nucleic acid therapeutics.
articles.abstract: An optimal nucleic acid delivery system for hepatic therapeutics should demonstrate consistent pharmacological performance across both normal and diseased hepatic microenvironments, enabling repeated administration with favorable safety profiles. Given the disease-sensitive and relatively low expression of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) on hepatocytes and compared to the abundant and disease-resilient expression of asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR), ASGPR-mediated drug delivery presents a compelling strategy for liver diseases. Here, we introduce Hepa-SENS, a next-generation polymer-lipid hybrid nanoparticle platform enabling robust ASGPR-mediated hepatocyte delivery without ligand conjugation. Its biodistribution, hepatocyte selectivity, receptor dependence, repeated-dose activity, and therapeutic performance were evaluated in healthy and fibrotic mouse liver models. Hepa-SENS demonstrates strong, hepatocyte-selective transgene expression of mRNA payload preserved under disease conditions, such as high-fatty liver and liver fibrosis, and across multiple species, including non-human primates. In long-term repeat-dose regimens, Hepa-SENS sustained mRNA-driven protein expression without inducing antibodies to the delivery system, enabling greater consistency than conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). In fact, in a liver fibrosis mouse model, where a reduction of LDLR is observed as fibrosis develops, Hepa-SENS outperformed conventional LNPs in delivering therapeutic hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha mRNA and attenuating disease progression. In conclusion, Hepa-SENS represents a robust and versatile delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics targeting hepatocytes under disease-relevant conditions via ASGPR-dependent mechanisms. Its repeated-dosing-compatible design supports durable treatment strategies for chronic liver diseases.

articles.title: Unraveling the multitarget mechanisms of aloe emodin against periodontitis: a synergy of network pharmacology and experimental validation.
